name: Sydney
description: Central Sydney, a harbour city of sails and sandstone: the Opera House on Bennelong Point, the Harbour Bridge, The Rocks where the colony began, and the ferries of Circular Quay.

terrain.attribution: NSW Spatial Services NSW_5M_Elevation, 5 m bare earth from stereo imagery (CC BY 4.0)

bridges.note: Darling Harbour's bridges; the wharves' and pontoons' gangways float and are left out.

Pyrmont Bridge.note: 1902, timber Allan trusses and the steel swing span

seawall.note: Sydney Harbour and Darling Harbour: Hawkesbury sandstone ashlar and its concrete repairs under a sandstone or concrete coping; the tide ranges about 1.8 m.

water.note: Sydney Harbour is mapped as a water polygon (Port Jackson); the Overture ocean polygon stops at the Heads.

waves.note: A typical afternoon north-easterly sea breeze over the 4 km reach from Bradleys Head to the bridge; chosen values, not a measurement.

water.colour_note: Harbour water has a few metres of visibility. Seen from the air on a clear day it reads a deep blue, teal near the shore: the colours and the light the water gives back (scatter) were matched to aerial photographs of the Opera House (Wikimedia Commons, "Sydney (AU), Opera House -- 2019 -- 2896.jpg"). The NSW aerial photo, taken straight down, shows it darker and greener.

tussock.note: Tussock (trees.json tussock, #315, #326): the native grasses of Barangaroo Reserve's headland (its list, barangaroo.com Botany: Themeda, Poa and Danthonia among its 84 Sydney species; 68,000 grasses were planted), in the Reserve's own planted beds only: OpenStreetMap's natural=scrub inside its outline, not its named lawns, paths and sandstone (Overture base land, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; pipeline/grasses.py). Tinted from the shared snow tussock's straw to their green. The parks and the Domain are mown lawn, so none there.

lomandra.note: Lomandra (trees.json lomandra, #326): spiny-headed mat-rush, Lomandra longifolia, the strappy tussock among the Reserve's grasses (6,000 of them in its planting), in the same beds (OpenStreetMap's natural=scrub inside Barangaroo Reserve; pipeline/grasses.py).

trees.note: The mix is the City of Sydney inventory's (trees.survey) species shares by genus: its street trees for mix (gums: brush box, water gum, paperbarks, eucalypts and angophoras 31%, plane trees 25%, deciduous broadleaves 20.5% as elm, evergreen broadleaves 10.7%, figs 5.4%, jacarandas 3.4%, palms 3%, she-oaks 0.9% as casuarina), its park trees for woods.

survey.attribution: City of Sydney, Trees (CC BY 4.0), extracted 2026-11-07: the street and park trees it surveys, with their measured heights

areas.name: First Fleet Park
areas.note: First Fleet Park, between the Museum of Contemporary Art and the wharves: Destination NSW's jacaranda trail names it as the place to see them against the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House (sydney.com, 'Where to see jacarandas in Sydney'). The council's inventory surveys its street trees, not the park's, so the park's mix is the trail's jacarandas with a few figs and palms.

areas.name: Circular Quay West, by the MCA
areas.note: The promenade between the Museum of Contemporary Art and the water: Destination NSW's photographs of the trail show 'jacarandas outside the Museum of Contemporary Art, Circular Quay'. Not in the council's inventory, so its trees take the trail's jacarandas.

areas.name: Wendy Whiteley's Secret Garden
areas.note: Wendy Whiteley's garden on the old railway land above Lavender Bay: Moreton Bay figs, palms and jacarandas, the Harbour Bridge beyond.

protection.title: Sydney LEP 2012, clause 6.18
protection.summary: Development may not add to the total shadow on these public places across their protected hours.
protection.source_note: Protected windows as amended by Amendment No 64. The NSW legislation site refused automated access, so they were transcribed from secondary sources; check the official text before relying on them. Places without a verified window show sun now but are not tested.
protection.reading_note: Two readings matter more than any data error. Times: the Standard Time Act 1987 is reported to read times in legal instruments as standard time, which during daylight saving is an hour later on the clock; for Macquarie Place that changes the sun in its window by up to 44 points. Baseline: the clause compares against buildings existing at a fixed date, while this test compares against today's model.
protection.tip: Tip: try the block west of Hyde Park, or just north of Martin Place.

reference_heights.source: Wikipedia, List of tallest buildings in Sydney (October 2026)

tour.title: Sydney Harbour
tour.text: Gadigal Country, where the First Fleet dropped anchor in 1788. Today the harbour is the city's living room: ferries crossing, sails on the water, and a flat white on the quay.

tour.title: Sydney Opera House
tour.text: Jørn Utzon's sails, each shell cut from a single sphere, covered in a million Swedish tiles that wash themselves in the rain. Catch a show, or just sit on the steps at sunset.

tour.title: Sydney Harbour Bridge
tour.text: The Coathanger, opened in 1932: climb the arch 134 m above the water, walk across from The Rocks to Milsons Point, or watch the fireworks pour off it at New Year.

tour.title: Winter among the towers
tour.text: In June the sun stays low over the city and the towers throw long shadows across the streets. The light is gold all day: a good season for the harbour walk from the Quay to the Botanic Garden.

tour.title: Martin Place at lunchtime
tour.text: The city's grand plaza, where Sydney eats its lunch on the steps. On a winter lunchtime {sun:Martin Place|6-21|12:30}% of it is in the sun; in December, {sun:Martin Place|12-21|12:30}%.

tour.title: Hyde Park
tour.text: Avenues of fig trees and the Archibald Fountain, the oldest park in Australia. In winter its sunny lawns shrink from {sun:Hyde Park|6-21|10:00}% at 10:00 to {sun:Hyde Park|6-21|14:00}% by 14:00.

tour.title: Sydney Tower
tour.text: The gold turret at 309 m, the city's tallest since 1981. On a clear day the Blue Mountains show from the observation deck, and the restaurant up top slowly turns the whole city past your table.

tour.title: After dark
tour.text: The city lights up window by window and the bridge glows over the water. Drag to explore, or open Sun access to test a tower of your own.

rail_osm.note: The City Circle's two tracks over Circular Quay and the station's platform edges (pipeline/rail_osm.py -> cities/sydney/rail_osm.json; cities/sydney/rail.py builds the station and the trains' courses from it).

fishing.note: Fishing from the shore (docs/FISHING.md, pipeline/fishing.py). Legal lengths, bag limits and the food advice are NSW DPI's; where each fish holds and when it bites is anglers' lore turned into weights chosen for the game, and the lengths are usual ranges, not a survey.

rules.licence: NSW asks anyone fishing for a Recreational Fishing Fee receipt, and for each fish to be measured against its legal length.
rules.release: Every fish here goes back: the game keeps a log, not a bag.

zones.name: East of the Harbour Bridge
zones.advice: East of the bridge the advice is to eat no more than 150 g of harbour fish a month.

zones.name: West of the Harbour Bridge
zones.advice: West of the bridge nothing caught should be eaten, and catches are to be released. Commercial fishing in the harbour has been closed since 2006.

rigs.name: Prawn under a float
rigs.hint: Close to the wall and the piles, for whatever is feeding there.

rigs.name: Soft plastic on the bottom
rigs.hint: Hopped slowly over the sand for flathead and bream.

rigs.name: Metal lure, cast long
rigs.hint: Out into the current for tailor, trevally and kingfish.

species.name: Yellowtail scad
species.note: Yakkas school round every wharf in the harbour. Most are caught to be bait for something bigger.

species.name: Fan-bellied leatherjacket
species.note: A small mouth and a beak of teeth: it picks a bait off the hook a nibble at a time before it takes it.

species.name: Yellowfin bream
species.note: The harbour's everyday fish, hard against the piles and the oyster-covered rocks, and boldest in low light.

species.name: Luderick
species.note: Blackfish graze the weed on the walls and take a float down slowly. Winter is their season.

species.name: Silver trevally
species.note: Pound for pound the hardest puller on the wharf: it turns side-on and circles all the way in.

species.name: Tailor
species.note: Named for teeth that cut a bait as cleanly as scissors. Schools hunt the harbour at dusk.

species.name: Dusky flathead
species.note: It lies buried in the sand and waits. Over 70 cm it is a breeding female, and the law sends it back.

species.name: Yellowtail kingfish
species.note: The harbour's prize. A hooked king runs for the nearest pile or mooring chain to cut the line on it.

spots.name: Beulah Street Wharf
spots.note: A small public wharf in Kirribilli, straight across from the Opera House. The piles hold yellowtail and trevally, and kingfish come past in summer.
spots.source: Man of Many, Best fishing spots in Sydney (Beulah Street Wharf: squid, yellowtail, trevally)

spots.name: Blues Point Reserve
spots.note: The point at the foot of Blues Point Road, with the bridge to the east and deep water off the rocks. It is west of the bridge, so nothing caught here is for the table.
spots.source: Man of Many, Best fishing spots in Sydney (Blues Point Reserve: trevally, kingfish, jewfish)

game.title: Sydney on Foot
game.blurb: Walk Sydney under the real sun. Talk to the people who know it, ride the ferries round the harbour, and fly under the Harbour Bridge.
game.under_bridge_note: 49 m of clearance, and you used it.

ferry_style.note: Sydney Ferries' green and cream with a gold band; the dimensions are approximate.

climate.source: Bureau of Meteorology, Sydney (Observatory Hill) 066062, mean maximum temperature 1859-2020

game.ferry_note: Wharves and the helipad are from OpenStreetMap via Overture. Routes are generated through open water, and the stops follow the inner-harbour services, but the timetable is not real. Ferries run at 1.5 times their real speed (9 m/s) and wait 20 s at each wharf. The vessel names are those of the First Fleet class ferries. At a wharf you can skip the wait.

vehicles.note: The helicopter, ferries and cars are shared by every city (web/assets/vehicles, built by blender/build_vehicles.py). Pick a livery from vehicles.json or give your own colours; the registration defaults to the country's. The ferries take their colours and length from ferry_style.

cars.note: Sydney's taxis come in any colour, mostly white, silver or black, with a roof sign; the buses are white with a blue band (approximate).

travel.name: Jacaranda lookout, Circular Quay
travel.note: Above Circular Quay station, where the Cahill Walk looks over the quay: First Fleet Park's jacarandas below, the Harbour Bridge ahead and the Opera House across the water, the view of the postcards (sydney.com, 'Where to see jacarandas in Sydney'). Out of season, arriving moves the date into the bloom.

travel.name: Jacaranda walk, by the MCA
travel.note: Under the jacarandas on Circular Quay West, outside the Museum of Contemporary Art, looking across the quay to the Opera House.

flocks.name: Silver gulls
flocks.note: Silver gulls (Chroicocephalus novaehollandiae) are common throughout Australia: 40 to 45 cm long, with a white head, tail and underparts, a light grey back and black-tipped wings, and in adults a bright orange-red bill, legs and eye-ring. They readily pester people for scraps and pilfer from unattended food (Australian Museum). Juveniles have brown patterns on their wings and a dark bill (Wikipedia). The flock, its box of hot chips and where it works the broadwalk by the Opera Bar are a game scene, not a survey.
flocks.source: Australian Museum, Silver Gull; Wikipedia, Silver gull

npcs.name: Ava
idle: The Manly ferry goes from Wharf 3. Half an hour across the harbour, and the best view in Sydney for the price of a ticket.
There are five trig stations round the harbour, a triangle on the map for each. Climb up to one for the view.

npcs.name: Marco
idle: Each shell is a triangle cut from one sphere, 75.2 m in radius. Utzon's 'spherical solution', 1961.
Mind your chips on the broadwalk. The gulls by the Opera Bar will have them out of your hand.

npcs.name: Lena
idle: The arch spans 503 m. The deck is {landmark:harbour_bridge.deck_width_m} m wide and 49 m above the water.

npcs.name: Sam
idle: Under the deck, keep it below 45 m. The rotor needs the room.

npcs.name: Priya
idle: Martin Place is protected from 1 September to 31 May, 12:00 to 14:00. Winter isn't covered.

npcs.name: Tom
idle: The Archibald Fountain's been here since 1932. A newspaperman left the money, to remember France and Australia in the Great War.
Think you can judge a height by eye? Aim at a building and press G. I'm usually out by twenty metres.

npcs.name: Noor
idle: Barangaroo Reserve was a container wharf until 2015. Now it's sandstone and fig trees.
It's {time} here. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Kev
idle: Bream under the bridge in the mornings. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Jess
idle: Forty to forty-five centimetres of gull, and every one of them knows where the chips are.
It's {time} here. {sun_line}

npcs.name: Dee
idle: Best platform in Sydney, this one. I've missed trains on purpose just to watch the ferries come in.
Platform 2 goes round by St James and Museum, platform 1 by Wynyard and Town Hall. Either way you end up at Central.

npcs.name: Bill
idle: Opened in 1956, the last piece of the City Circle. They had the tunnels dug either side thirty years before the station was built.
The road on our roof is the Cahill Expressway. People have wanted it gone since the day it opened, and it's still the best free lookout on the quay.
Stand behind the yellow line, mate. The double-deckers come in quicker than you'd think.

npcs.name: Mia
idle: Bridge on the left, Opera House on the right, a ferry in the middle. I don't even need to leave the station.
They say come at dusk, when the sky goes pink behind the bridge.

lines.title: Report back
lines.on_open: All three walks done. Report back to Ava at Circular Quay.

quests.title: Welcome to the Quay
talk: G'day, welcome to the Quay! I'm Ava; I show people round the harbour. It's {season} here, and the water looks good {now}.

Three walks, any order. The harbour: Marco at the Opera House, then a ferry and the bridge. The air: Sam flies from the Kirribilli helipad. The ground: Priya, in Martin Place, knows where the sun falls at lunch.

The helicopter's on the lawn of First Fleet Park behind you, ferries leave from the wharves along the quay, and a hand up at the kerb (Y) stops a taxi. WASD to walk, E to talk, T to switch walks. Which first?

choices.text: The harbour: Marco, at the Opera House
The air: Sam, at the Kirribilli helipad
The ground: Priya, in Martin Place

quests.title: Shells from one sphere
talk: Ava sent you? Welcome. Look up: every one of these shells is a spherical triangle cut from one sphere, 75.2 m in radius.
The highest stands 67 m above the water. The tiles came from Sweden, over a million of them, in gloss white and matt cream.
First, climb the Monumental Steps up to the podium. They're nearly 100 m wide, and everyone who comes here sits on them.
Then see the harbour from the water. Take a ferry from Circular Quay, Wharf 4, to Milsons Point. Lena will meet you there.

steps.text: Climb the Monumental Steps to the podium
Take a ferry from Circular Quay to Milsons Point

quests.title: Over the arch
talk: Nice ride? Now look up. The arch spans 503 m, and its crown is 134 m above the water.
Walk up the approach from here to the middle of the arch. Locals call it the Coathanger.
That's the harbour done once you're up there. Sam keeps a helicopter at the Kirribilli helipad, along the shore, if you want to see it from above.

steps.text: Walk up onto the bridge and reach the middle of the arch

quests.title: Under the bridge
talk: Ava said you'd come. Hop in. The helicopter's on the pad.
Fly under the bridge deck. It clears the water by 49 m, so stay below 45. Then set down in the Domain.
Space to climb, C to descend, W and S for forward and back, A and D to turn. V switches to a bird's-eye view. E gets you out once you've landed.

steps.text: Fly under the Harbour Bridge deck

quests.title: A place in the sun
talk: The planning rule says new towers may not add shadow to Martin Place between 12:00 and 14:00, from September to May.
Winter isn't protected. On 21 June at 12:30, only {sun:Martin Place|6-21|12:30}% of the place gets direct sun. On 21 December it's {sun:Martin Place|12-21|12:30}%.
Find a sunny spot here at lunchtime on 21 June, like the office workers do. The sun meter under the map tells you when you're in it.

steps.text: Stand in direct sun in Martin Place, 12:00 to 14:00 on 21 June

quests.title: Hyde Park
talk: Priya sent you? Sit down a minute. Governor Macquarie named Hyde Park in 1810, and the colony ran its first horse races here that same year. It's the oldest public park in the country.
The fig avenue runs right down the middle. And across College Street is St Mary's: they only finished its spires in 2000, a hundred and thirty years after they started.
Go and stand under them.

steps.text: Cross College Street to St Mary's Cathedral

quests.title: Hot chips at the Quay
talk: Watch your chips! See that lot down by the water? Silver gulls. Everyone calls them seagulls.
White head and tail, a light grey back, black-tipped wings, and the bill, legs and eye-ring a bright orange-red. The ones with brown on their wings and a dark bill are young.

Someone's dropped a box of hot chips on the broadwalk, so that's lunch for the whole flock. The Australian Museum says they're 'readily pestering humans for handouts of scraps'. Look away and they're in your box.
Go and have a look. Just don't feed them.

steps.text: Walk up to the gulls fighting over the chips by the water

quests.title: The harbour city
talk: That's the lot: the water, the bridge, the air and the sun at lunchtime. You've seen more of it in a day than most of us do in a year.
The city's yours. Change the time of day, take any ferry, or fly anywhere. Sunset on the Opera House steps is hard to beat.
